chapter: Opinions on singers, promotion and originality
title: Originators and imitators: who gets credit
summary: Edison and Dance discuss credit for black originators like Hawkins, Armstrong and Ellington while whites copy.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, you know, it's a very difficult
subject because, you know, I've always said that as far as I'm concerned --
Who's contributed anymore to the world of art than Duke Ellington?
Well, but you constantly -- you know, you can say all of the great innovators of jazz have been black and they will agree.
I would say originators. Because they have -- the whole world can recognize them from the first sound. And anybody that sounds like the originator after that is an imitator.
So then, okay, you invent this. And white musicians are naturally going to play it. I mean, the white musicians like it --
They like it, they're going to play it. Well now, they play it filtered through their --
-- racial feeling or whatever, and that dilution is naturally -- I mean, this is not necessarily prejudice, it's more than likely going to appeal to white people.
You know, because it's diluted a little bit.
Well, why don't they give the originator

Why don't they give him the credit while he's living, while he's originating, like they do a Thomas Edison? To me, the originator, like Coleman Hawkins, is just as great as Thomas Edison, to me. To me he is because in his field he originated something on the tenor saxophone, you know.

Never been heard before. Louis Armstrong, he broke all the rules of trumpet. Duke, he broke all the rules of arranging. They said, you cannot play dissonant chords because it's displeasing to the ear. Duke played them and made everybody listen.
